name: Cape Hatteras National Seashore
author: author-B-2026-10-18
summary:
A thin, broken strand of barrier islands curves out into the Atlantic and back again, sheltering North Carolina’s mainland coast and sounds. For thousands of years these islands of the Outer Banks have survived wind and sea; Cape Hatteras National Seashore protects their beaches, dunes, marshes and maritime forests of oak, cedar and yaupon holly. Offshore lie the shifting sand ridges of Diamond Shoals, in waters called the Graveyard of the Atlantic: more than 600 ships wrecked here, the park brochure counts, and in World War II German submarines sank so many Allied ships that the area was also called Torpedo Junction. Villagers served in the U.S. Life-Saving Service from the 1870s, kept the lighthouses — Ocracoke’s of 1823, Cape Hatteras’s of 1870, Bodie Island’s of 1872 — and buried the dead when rescues failed. [1]

Congress authorized Cape Hatteras as the first national seashore in 1937, and it was formally established on January 12, 1953. [1] [1] It stretches more than 70 miles across Bodie, Hatteras and Ocracoke islands; eight villages that predate the park lie among them but are not part of it. The park’s 2011 foundation document lists those who have made these islands home — Native Americans, farmers, watermen, enslaved people, lighthouse keepers and surfmen — and calls the seashore a living laboratory for the study of climate change and its effects on sea level. [1]

indigenous.html: The first written account of the Outer Banks, Verrazzano’s of 1524, tells of many Native people meeting his crew off what was likely Hatteras Island; in David Stick’s 1958 retelling, they hauled a sailor tumbled by the surf onto dry sand and later sent him back to his boat. In 1590 John White speculated that the lost Roanoke colonists had joined the friendly Indians at Croatoan, now Hatteras Island — a theory never substantiated. The park’s 2005 ethnohistory reports that in the early 1700s about 80 Indians, likely Hatteras, lived in the Cape Woods along the sound; the archaeological record suggests theirs were the island’s only permanent settlements. Quoting Gary Dunbar (1956), it says they were described in 1715 as “in great poverty,” and that a 1733 cartographer counted “6 or 8” at Hatteras living among the English. Stick found the last reference to the Hatteras Indians in a 1788 deed from “Mary Elks, Inden, of Hatteras Banks.” [1]

sources.title: Impact Assessment, Inc., Ethnohistorical Description of the Eight Villages adjoining Cape Hatteras National Seashore and Interpretive Themes of History and Heritage, Vol. 1 (NPS, November 2005)

black.html: Slave ownership on the Banks was minimal but present; under Union occupation during the Civil War Hatteras Island held about 1,200 people, almost 100 of them enslaved, by historian David Stick’s count. [1] Richard Etheridge, born enslaved, who had served three years in the army’s 36th Infantry (colored), became on January 24, 1880, the first African American to command a life-saving station when he was named keeper of the Pea Island station, after its all-white crew was dismissed for negligence following an 1879 wreck. His all-Black crew — the only all-Black life-saving station in the country — rescued all nine people aboard the schooner E.S. Newman in a storm on October 11, 1896. The crew went unrecognized during the station’s years of service; on March 5, 1996, Etheridge and six surfmen were posthumously awarded Gold Lifesaving Medals. [1]

climate.html: Most of the seashore’s barrier islands are less than 400 meters wide and lie entirely within the 100-year flood zone, and the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2005 assessment found relative sea level at Beaufort, about 75 kilometers southwest of Ocracoke, rising about 3.7 millimeters a year — roughly twice the global average — and rated 27 percent of the nearly 120 miles of shoreline it evaluated at very high vulnerability to sea-level rise and another 27 percent at high. [1] At Cape Hatteras, the 2003 cultural landscape report says, erosion had claimed about 1,800 feet of beach in front of the original 1803 tower by 1872; in 1999 the entire light station was moved southwest to a site about 1,600 feet from the shoreline. [1]

labor_ccc.html: In the early 1930s North Carolina planned three parallel lines of ocean-front dunes from the Virginia line to Ocracoke Inlet, and the work was turned over to the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Work Projects Administration. [1] Crews erected sand fences, piled brush from trees downed in the 1933 storm along the beach to trap sand, planted grass and dug roads and ditches; islanders recall camps at Rodanthe, near the Cape Hatteras lighthouse and on Ocracoke, where workers built theirs from lumber salvaged from the 1935 wreck of the Nomis. Some of the young men, paid $30 a month, married local women and stayed. [1] Near the lighthouse, the 2003 cultural landscape report finds, the CCC and WPA dunes of 1935–36 held the shoreline back for thirty years. [1]

Ocracoke Lighthouse 1823 (NC's oldest operating); Cape Hatteras Lighthouse 1870; Bodie Island Lighthouse 1872

Verrazzano 1524 first written account; anchored off what was likely Hatteras Island; a large number of native people; sailor hauled to dry sand, fire, sent back (Stick 1958, as retold in the ethnohistory)
John White 1590 speculated colonists joined the 'friendly Indians at Croatoan, now Hatteras Island'; never substantiated

Early 1700s about 80 Indians in the Cape Woods along the Sound, likely of the Hatteras culture; archaeological record suggests the only permanent settlements on the island; 1715 'in great poverty'; 1733 cartographer '6 or 8 (Indians) at Hatteras, who dwell among the English' (Dunbar 1956) — reported only as quoted, no survival/extinction claim made
Last reference to the Hatteras Indians a 1788 deed from 'Mary Elks, Inden, of Hatteras Banks' (Stick 1958)
Slave ownership minimal but present (Stick 1958); under Federal occupation some 1,200 people on Hatteras Island including almost 100 slaves (Stick 1958, 154)
Richard Etheridge born as a slave; served 3 years in the army, 36th inft (colored); appointed keeper January 24, 1880; first African American to command a Life-Saving station
1879 Henderson wreck; all-white crew dismissed for negligence; replaced by all-black crew with Etheridge as keeper; the only all African-American life-saving station in the U.S.

October 11, 1896 schooner E.S. Newman; rescued all nine passengers and crew; keeper and six surfmen awarded Gold Lifesaving Medals posthumously March 5, 1996; crew unrecognized during its years of service

Barriers mostly <400 m wide, entirely within the 100-year flood zone; relative sea-level rise at Beaufort (about 75 km SW of Ocracoke) 3.71 ± 0.64 mm/yr, approximately 2 times the global average; nearly 195 km (120 mi) of shoreline evaluated, 27% very high, 27% high vulnerability
By 1872 beach erosion had claimed approximately 1,800 feet in front of the 1803 tower

In 1999 International Chimney Corporation moved the entire light station southwest to a site approximately 1,600 feet from the shoreline (CLR gives 2,500 feet moved; nps.gov 'Moving the Lighthouse' gives 2,900 feet — distance omitted from text because sources disagree)
Early 1930s state plan for three parallel lines of ocean-front dunes from the NC-Virginia border to Ocracoke Inlet; project turned over to the CCC and WPA (MacNeill 1958)

CCC erected sand fences, collected brush from 1933 storm, dug roads and ditches, planted trees and spartina; camps at Rodanthe (barges), Cape Hatteras (cabins south of the lighthouse) and Ocracoke (built from lumber salvaged from the Nomis wreck of 1935), per villager recollections; $30 per month; some married local girls and stayed
1935–36 artificial dunes by CCC and WPA provided thirty years of protection by halting the westward movement of the shoreline (at the light station)
